title: Monitor and manage the cold chain in perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Cold chain documentation and the cooling cycle
lessons.html:
Logistical documentation in the cold chain

Documents carry the instructions and evidence that keep the cold chain compliant. A cold chain manager must know what each contains and which sections matter most.

DocumentSections that ensure compliance
Shipping or temperature instructionProduct, cultivar, set point, ventilation, humidity, CA settings, any stepped regime, cold treatment requirement
Booking with the shipping lineContainer type, set point, ventilation and special requirements passed to the line
Pallet records and packing listPallet numbers, product, PUC and PHC codes, linking product to container
PPECB inspection and export certificationProof of APS Act compliance and inspection result
Container inspection and loading recordsContainer condition, pre-cooling, pulp temperatures at loading, probe and logger positions
Phytosanitary certificateProduct, quantity, treatments declared, for the importing country
Temperature recordsCold store logs, container download, cold treatment probe records

The most common errors are a wrong set point on the booking, a cold treatment not flagged, or pallet numbers that do not match the container. Each can cause rejection or loss, so documents must be cross-checked before loading.

Operational requirements for an effective cooling cycle

  • Minimise field heat time: get fruit from orchard to cooling quickly and keep it shaded.
  • Use the right cooling method: forced-air cooling for most packed fruit; hydrocooling for some stone fruit and vegetables; room cooling only to hold already cold product.
  • Correct packaging and stacking: vents aligned, pallets placed so air is forced through the cartons, not around them; tarpaulins or baffles to seal gaps.
  • Adequate capacity: refrigeration capacity and fan power sized for peak daily intake.
  • Monitor progress: pulp temperature probes in representative cartons, including the warmest positions, until the target is reached.
  • Avoid over-cooling: do not cool below the safe temperature for chilling-sensitive products.
  • Move to holding rooms once cooled, without warming during transfer.

Cooling is often described in terms such as half-cooling time and seven-eighths cooling time, which help managers compare and plan cooling capacity.

lessons.title: Refrigeration management and equipment certification
lessons.html:
Applying refrigeration management practices

  • Set points and control: set points must follow the approved regime for each product. Check that controllers are reading correctly against calibrated reference thermometers.
  • Delivery and return air: monitor both. A large difference indicates heavy heat load or air flow problems.
  • Defrost management: evaporators must defrost regularly to keep air flowing; ice build-up reduces capacity.
  • Humidity: keep relative humidity high for most fruit to limit water loss, while avoiding free water.
  • Air flow: leave space between pallets and walls, do not block evaporator fans, and do not overload rooms.
  • Door discipline: keep doors closed, use strip curtains and fast doors, and load from sealed docks.
  • Ethylene and mixing: do not mix ethylene producers with sensitive products.
  • Maintenance and back-up: planned maintenance on compressors, condensers and fans; generators and alarms for power failures.
  • Refrigerant safety: ammonia plants must have leak detection, emergency procedures and trained staff.

Inspecting and certifying cold chain equipment

Cold stores, precoolers, containers and vessels used for export must be inspected and approved as the PPECB requirements specify. A cold chain inspection typically checks:

  • Structure: insulation, doors, seals, floors and drains in good condition; clean and odour-free.
  • Refrigeration performance: able to pull down and hold the set point.
  • Instrumentation: temperature sensors, recorders and probes present, working and calibrated; records available.
  • Containers: pre-trip inspection completed, unit set to the correct set point and ventilation, pre-cooled where required, drains and door seals intact.
  • Cold treatment facilities: correct number of probes, calibrated and positioned as the protocol requires.

Instrument calibration

Thermometers and probes are checked against a reference, for example in an ice-water mixture or against a certified reference thermometer, at set intervals. Results and any corrections are recorded. A probe that reads half a degree wrong can invalidate a cold treatment or hide a chilling risk.

lessons.title: Loading inspection, temperature management and supervision
lessons.html:
Inspecting product for loading approval

Before a container or vessel hold is loaded, the product and the transport unit are checked:

  1. Documents: pallet numbers, products and quantities match the booking and instructions.
  2. Pulp temperatures: measured with calibrated probes in sample cartons from several pallets and positions. Product must be at or near its required carrying temperature; warm product should not be loaded, because containers are designed to hold temperature, not to cool warm fruit quickly.
  3. Product condition: no visible damage, wet or collapsed cartons, or decay.
  4. Pallet build: correct height, corner boards, strapping and labels.
  5. Container readiness: pre-cooled, clean, set correctly, with loggers and probes ready.

Temperature management practices

  • Record temperatures at each handover: packhouse, transport, port cold store, terminal and loading.
  • Use data loggers that travel with the product and are downloaded at destination.
  • Set alarm limits and respond to alarms quickly.
  • Minimise time on docks and at the port; pre-plan loading sequences.
  • For cold treatment, verify probes are inserted into fruit at the specified positions and that records show continuous compliance.
  • Analyse temperature records after each shipment to find weak links.

Supervising cold chain handling

The cold chain manager supervises people as much as machines. Responsibilities include:

  • training forklift drivers, loaders and cold store staff on why speed and door discipline matter;
  • setting and checking standard times, for example maximum minutes on a dock;
  • planning shifts so that receiving, cooling and loading do not clash;
  • investigating deviations, writing corrective actions and following them up;
  • communicating with exporters, transporters, terminals and shipping lines.

Example: data logger downloads show that pallets on one route consistently warm by several degrees between the packhouse and the port. Investigation shows the transporter switches off the refrigeration unit during a long stop. The manager addresses this in the transport contract, requires unit downloads, and the problem disappears.

Key points

  • Cross-check shipping instructions, bookings and pallet records before loading.
  • Effective cooling needs fast field-to-cooler time, correct stacking and monitoring.
  • Cold chain equipment must be inspected, approved and calibrated.
  • Do not load warm product; containers hold temperature, they do not precool.
  • Use temperature records at every handover to find and fix weak links.
